new_statements.quote: The Mahakiranti language Kham (Watters 2002) is a fully tonal language with no reference to stress or accent. It has a four tone system, divided over two registers that originate from phonation differences in consonants. The tonal distinction in each register predates the register distinction and may itself originate from an accent–no accent opposition.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only. The 2010 survey reports that Watters' grammar describes Kham as fully tonal (2 melodies x 2 phonation registers = 4 tones) and makes no reference to word stress or accent. The AUTOTYP word-domain database, coding the same grammar as 'Grammar Explicit', instead records exactly one main stress per grammatical word (stem ± prefixes ± suffixes) that targets a long vowel, i.e. a weight-sensitive placement. The two second-hand reports conflict and neither gives a page; the primary text (Watters 2002 ch. 2-3) could not be opened. First-hand sources that were opened (Watters 2003 chapter, Watters 1985 article, Noonan 2005 review) describe tone, syllable weight (bimoraic minimal word) and downstep but state no stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: AUTOTYP's stress domain is the grammatical word (stem ± prefix ± suffix); Watters 2003 gives the tone domain as the word base (root + derivational morphemes) with inflectional suffixes carrying separate tone. All descriptions are of the Takale dialect (citation forms in a grammar), not of an Eastern Parbate variety.
new_statements.identity_note: All existing descriptions of 'Kham' (Watters 1971, 1985, 1998, 2002, 2003, 2004; Noonan 2005) are of the Takale dialect (Taka village, Rukum), which Glottolog 5.3 files as taka1261 under Western Parbate Kham (west2420, ISO kjl); WALS (kmh) and AUTOTYP (LID 664) also map 'Kham' to west2420. Glottolog lists only the overview pp. 11-14 of Watters 2002 under east2354, whose sole listed dialect is Bhujel Kham (bhuj1238). Watters 2003 places Maikoti, Jangkoti, Tapnangi, Tamali, Nishel, Bhujel etc. in Eastern Parbate; no phonological description of any of these varieties was found. Any stress statement recovered from Watters would therefore be a Western Parbate (Takale) statement applied to east2354 by extension.

new_statements.quote: In polysyllabic morphemes, all syllables can be short, but not all can be long. If there is a long syllable somewhere in the string it will usually be the final syllable, though there are some exceptions. Furthermore, stress will fall on that final, long syllable (though this is not to be equated with high pitch). In a bisyllabic morpheme in which both syllables are open and short there is no discernible stress placement [...] In trisyllabic morphemes [...] in which all syllables are open and short, there is discernible stress on the final syllable (in spite of its shortness) [...] Where the first syllable is long [...] the stress falls on the long syllable, not the final one

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for east2354. The one statement held by the project, Schiering & van der Hulst 2010:586 ('Kham (Watters 2002) is a fully tonal language with no reference to stress or accent'), is contradicted as a characterization of the source: Watters 2002:23 does refer to stress and gives a placement rule (long syllable, else final in trisyllables, none discernible in light disyllables), while agreeing that Kham is tonal and that stress is not pitch. It agrees with AUTOTYP WordDomains LID 664 (west2420) 'Exactly 1 Main Stress V:' sourced to this grammar, and is consistent with Watters 1985's remark on unstressed prefix syllables. Identity: the rule is stated for Takale Kham (taka1261,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Within a polysyllabic morpheme (Takale Kham) at most one syllable is long, normally the last, and stress falls on that long syllable; if instead the first syllable is long (rare) stress goes to it, not to the final (ká:sa, phó:sa, bé:pari). With no long syllable: trisyllabic all-light morphemes have final stress (buchulá, bokolá, dohkorá, gulyalí), disyllabic all-light morphemes show no discernible stress (kata, baza, gohga). Stress is explicitly distinguished from high pitch (the language is tonal: four-box tone system, chs. 1 and 3). I.e. quantity-sensitive, default-final, stated for the morpheme domain; AUTOTYP's coding 'Exactly 1 Main Stress V:' (stem +- affixes) is this passage.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (feed query 'secondary stress' in this volume: 0 hits); 2.4 snippet mentions an 'unstressed suffix' fusing with a monomoraic root into one bimoraic syllable (/kyo:/), i.e. suffixes are unstressed
new_statements.exceptions: 'though there are some exceptions' to the long syllable being final (then stress follows length, ex. (15)); all-light disyllables have 'no discernible stress placement'; many finally stressed long-final disyllables are said to derive from old C(r)/C(l) clusters with a schwa first vowel (ex. (16) bǝle..); stress 'is not to be equated with high pitch'
new_statements.identity_note: Watters 2002 describes Takale Kham, which Glottolog files as taka1261 under Western Parbate Kham (west2420, kjl), not under east2354. Eastern Parbate varieties (Nishel/Nisi, Maikoti, Bhujel Kham) appear in the grammar only in the dialect overview (1.6, pp. 11-14) and comparative morphology tables ('Takale and Nishel' Table 71 p. 162; 'three/four/five/seven Kham dialects' tables); the Contents shows no phonology, tone or stress section for any Eastern Parbate variety. Any stress statement eventually read from chs. 2-3 will be a Takale (west2420) statement applied to east2354 by proxy.

sources.citation: Watters, David E. 2003. Kham. In Graham Thurgood & Randy J. LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 683-704. London: Routledge. (Takale Kham)
sources.note: Section 2 Phonology (pp. 685-688) covers vowels, consonants, the syllable (weight by rhyme: V:, VV, VC all bimoraic; minimal word bimoraic; mentions 'rhythm groups') and tone (two melodies, marked 'accented' T1 vs 'neutral' T2, crossed with modal/lax register; downstep after T1 stems; tone domain = word base). No sentence states where word stress falls; the words 'stress'/'accent' occur only in 'accented tone (T1)'.

sources.citation: Noonan, Michael. 2005. Review of David E. Watters, A Grammar of Kham (Cambridge University Press, 2002). Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 28(1): 89-97.
sources.note: Summarises the grammar's phonology in one paragraph: Kham has a four-tone system (two tones distinguished by murmured/breathy voice), affixes regularly have independent tone, three places of articulation, front rounded vowels in Takale. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Watters, David E. 1985. Emergent word tone in Kham: a Tibeto-Burman halfway house. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 8(2): 36-54.
sources.note: Whole article is on tone (heightened pitch > downstep, recessive stems, word-tone emerging). 'Stress/unstressed' occurs only in paraphrasing Matisoff 1973 and Mazaudon 1976 on tone-shift mechanisms (pp. 36-37) and once on p. 51 ('equivalent to its destressing'); no statement of Kham word-stress placement.
